# Rubrics as Rewards: Reinforcement Learning Beyond Verifiable Domains
- **Core Insight:** GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B with a gpt-4o-mini judge that scores each response against a prompt-specific rubric (RaR-Implicit) reaches 31.2 on HealthBench versus 25.5 for a rubric-free Likert judge reward and 12.5 for four generic rubrics shared by all prompts, and 37.6 versus 34.8 mean accuracy on GPQA-Diamond (Fig. 2 bar labels); the authors summarize the gains over Likert rewards as up to 31% and 7% relative (Abstract, §5).
- **Guideline:** When RL targets open-ended expert tasks without a single verifiable answer, generate a rubric for each prompt conditioned on a reference answer and give the rubric to the judge, because on HealthBench-1k rubrics generated with reference answers (35.9) outperformed rubrics generated without them (32.0) and a Likert judge without rubrics (23.9) (§6, Table 1). This was tested only with a Qwen2.5-7B policy, 300 GRPO steps, and medicine and science data (§4.2, Table 10, §9).
- **Authors:** Anisha Gunjal, Anthony Wang, Elaine Lau, Vaskar Nath, Yunzhong He, Bing Liu, et al. (7 authors; Scale AI)
- **Year:** 2025 (arXiv v1 2025-07; v2 2025-10; arXiv comment: preprint)
- **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17746 (datasets: huggingface.co/datasets/anisha2102/RaR-Medicine, huggingface.co/datasets/anisha2102/RaR-Science)
- **Source type:** paper
- **Relevant topics:** rubric-based rewards, LLM-as-judge rewards, RL beyond verifiable domains, GRPO, reward aggregation, synthetic rubric generation, judge size, HealthBench, GPQA-Diamond

## Abstract
RLVR works for tasks with clear correctness signals such as math and code, but many real-world reasoning tasks are judged on several criteria at once. Instance-specific rubrics are already used in evaluation benchmarks. The paper introduces Rubrics as Rewards (RaR), an on-policy RL method that turns rubric feedback into rewards. In medicine and science, the authors compare several ways of aggregating rubric feedback. The best variant improves over LLM-as-judge baselines with direct Likert rewards by up to 31% relative on HealthBench and 7% on GPQA-Diamond. RaR-trained policies do well on both rubric-scored and multiple-choice evaluation, and rubric-structured rewards align smaller judges better with human preferences and reduce performance variance across judge scales (Abstract).

## Key Contributions
- A formulation with k weighted binary criteria per prompt and two aggregations: explicit (normalized weighted sum, Eq. 1) and implicit (the judge sees all criteria and returns one score, Eq. 2) (§2.2).
- Remark 1: RLVR is the special case k = 1, w_1 = 1, c_1 = match(y, ŷ) (§2.3, Eq. 3).
- Four rubric desiderata (expert grounding, coverage, criterion importance, self-contained items) and two released rubric datasets, RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science (§3, §4.1).
- Comparisons against Likert, reference-Likert, generic-rubric, and off-the-shelf baselines, plus a judge-alignment study (§5, Fig. 2-3).
- Ablations on rubric source (human vs synthetic, with or without reference), rubric elements, and the generator LLM (§6, Tables 1-3).

## Key Figures/Tables to Study
- **Figure 2** — HealthBench per-axis and overall scores; GPQA-Diamond mean accuracy with 95% CI.
- **Figure 3** — pairwise preference accuracy of judges of different sizes with and without rubrics.
- **Tables 1-3** — rubric source, rubric elements, generator LLM (HealthBench-1k).
- **Table 10 / Table 11** — GRPO hyperparameters; judge model used during training.
- **Appendix A.6 and the generation prompts** — judge prompts and rubric-writing prompts.

## Technical Details
**Explicit aggregation (§2.2, Eq. 1).** r(x, ŷ) = Σ_j w_j·c_j(x, ŷ) / Σ_j w_j. Here x is the prompt, ŷ a sampled response, k the number of criteria, w_j the weight of criterion j, and c_j(x, ŷ) ∈ {0, 1} a judge's decision that ŷ satisfies criterion j. Normalization makes rewards comparable across prompts with different rubric counts. RaR-Explicit maps labels to weights Essential 1.0, Important 0.7, Optional 0.3, Pitfall 0.9; pitfalls are phrased positively ("avoids ..."), so a satisfied pitfall adds reward (§4.4, footnote 3). Worked example (derived from Eq. 1): a response that meets one Essential and one Pitfall item and misses one Important item scores (1.0 + 0.9)/(1.0 + 0.7 + 0.9) = 1.9/2.6 = 0.73.

**Implicit aggregation (§2.2, Eq. 2; §4.4).** r_implicit(x, ŷ) = f_φ(x, ŷ, {d_j}), where f_φ is the LLM judge and d_j the criterion descriptions. The judge returns a 1-10 rating in JSON, normalized to [0, 1] (App. A.6).

**Rubric generation (§3.2, App. A generation prompts).**
1. An LLM writes 7-20 self-contained items per prompt, conditioned on the dataset's reference answer.
2. Each item has a title, a description starting with its category (Essential, Important, Optional, Pitfall), and a weight: 1-5 for Essential/Important/Optional and −1 or −2 for Pitfall.
3. Generators: GPT-4o for RaR-Medicine, o3-mini for RaR-Science (§4.1).

**Datasets (§4.1, App. A.1-A.2).** RaR-Medicine: 20,166 examples, 7.5 rubrics per question on average, 45.0 words per question; rubric types Important 34.1%, Essential 30.7%, Optional 22.1%, Pitfall 13.1%; Medical Diagnosis is 50.3% of topics (Tables 4-6). RaR-Science: 20,625 examples aligned with GPQA-Diamond categories, 7.5 rubrics, 52.6 words; Important 34.8%, Essential 28.4%, Optional 22.3%, Pitfall 14.5% (Tables 7-9; the Table 7 caption says "medical" for the science set). Prompt sources include natural_reasoning, SCP-116K, and GeneralThought-430K.

**Baselines (§4.3-4.4).** Direct-Likert: judge rates 1-10 without rubric or reference. Reference-Likert: judge rates 1-10 against a reference answer. RaR-Predefined: four generic rubrics for all prompts with uniform weights (App. A.5). Off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

**Evaluation (§4.5, App. A.7).** HealthBench: 5,000 clinical conversations with physician-written rubrics, greedy decoding; ablations hold out HealthBench-1k. GPQA-Diamond: 10 runs, greedy decoding, permuted answer choices, boxed-answer parsing with a GPT-4o verifier fallback, 95% CI. All policies are evaluated with gpt-4o-mini as the judge (Fig. 2 caption). Judge alignment: practitioner-approved answers paired with o3-perturbed answers that passed manual screening, 3,027 pairs (6,054 responses).

**Results.**
- Fig. 2 bar labels (read by x-position), HealthBench: Qwen2.5-7B 7.7, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 22.7, Direct-Likert 25.5, Reference-Likert 28.9, RaR-Predefined 12.5, RaR-Explicit 29.7, RaR-Implicit 31.2. GPQA-Diamond: 31.7, 35.0, 34.8, 36.5, 31.7, 36.9, 37.6 in the same order.
- The ratios of the RaR-Implicit and Direct-Likert labels are 1.22 (HealthBench) and 1.08 (GPQA-Diamond) (derived); the paper does not show which scores produce its stated 31% and 7%.
- Table 1 (train on 3.5k HealthBench prompts, test on HealthBench-1k): Expert-Answer-SFT 20.4, Simple-Likert 23.9, Reference-Likert 31.7, RaR-Implicit-Synthetic-NoRef 32.0, RaR-Implicit-Synthetic 35.9, RaR-Implicit-Human 34.8 (§6).
- Table 2 (o3-mini rubrics with reference): Essential-only 34.9, no categorical labels 38.8, no pitfall criteria 37.2, all rubrics 37.2. The authors note minimal differences from weights or pitfalls (§6).
- Table 3 (generators without reference answers): GPT-4o 34.2, GPT-4o-mini 32.7, o3-mini 32.4, Qwen-72B-Instruct 32.7, Qwen-32B-Instruct 31.1, Qwen-7B-Instruct 31.9; o3-mini with reference 35.9. The text states training on "the remaining 4k" HealthBench examples for this table (§6).
- Judge alignment: rubric guidance raises pairwise preference accuracy for every judge size, with the largest gains for smaller judges; synthetic rubrics without expert grounding fall between Likert and grounded rubrics (Fig. 3; values are in the figure image).
- Judge used during GRPO training (Table 11; the text calls the values judge accuracy on synthetic medical data and says rubrics yield stronger policies), RaR-Implicit vs Direct-Likert: GPT-4o-mini 27.9 vs 25.3; Qwen-32B-Instruct 26.2 vs 25.4; Qwen-14B-Instruct 25.0 vs 24.9; Qwen-7B-Instruct 26.7 vs 22.0; rubric-based scores span 0.250-0.279 vs 0.220-0.254 for Likert (App. A.8, Table 11).

## Findings relevant to generality and negative feedback
- **Transfer across evaluation formats:** RaR-Science training improves GPQA-Diamond multiple-choice accuracy; the authors conclude that rubric-induced skills generalize beyond rubric-based evaluation (§5; Interpretation).
- **Scope limits stated by the authors:** only medicine and science were tested; dialogue, tool use, and agentic tasks are not validated; only two aggregation strategies and off-the-shelf judges were used (§9).
- **Measurement:** gpt-4o-mini is both the training reward judge (§4.2) and the evaluation judge (Fig. 2 caption); no results with a different evaluation judge are reported. HealthBench-1k ablations train on other HealthBench prompts, and the authors state that in-domain testing amplifies RaR's gains (§6).
- **Negative criteria:** Pitfall items (13.1% and 14.5% of rubric items, Tables 5 and 8) lower the reward when unsatisfied (footnote 3). Removing them leaves HealthBench-1k unchanged at 37.2 (Table 2); the authors suggest synthetic pitfalls may lack specificity (§6; Interpretation). Rewards enter GRPO's group advantage computation (Fig. 1), so below-group rubric scores act as negative advantages (negative as gradient; course interpretation).

## Verification
- Created on 2026-09-14 from https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17746 (arXiv v2, 2025-10-03; v1 2025-07-23). Fig. 2 bar labels were read from the PDF text layer and assigned to methods by x-position.
- Audit claims not found in the source: "supplies the reward mechanism that Qwen3 General RL and the Kimi K2 rubric critic depend on" (the paper cites neither Qwen3 nor Kimi K2).
- Version differences: v1 reports "up to 28% relative improvement on HealthBench-1k", a numeric Table 1 with GPQA-Diamond means over 4 runs, and a Pitfall weight of 0.8; this card uses v2.
- Not reported by the source: KL and clipping settings, compute time, results at policy sizes other than 7B, evaluation with a judge other than gpt-4o-mini, numeric values of Fig. 3.
